speechtext: Mr. Speaker, before the Orders of the Day are called, I desire to ask a question with regard to the correspondence which took place on the subject of the inter-imperial conference. I am informed that the question was put to the right hon. the Premier (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier) a few days ago whether he would endeavour to have this correspondence laid on the Table at an early day, and he replied that he hoped to be able to lay it on the Table in a few days. Might I ask, in the absence of the leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden, Halifax), if the Prime Minister has any further information to give us on the subject ?

I told my hon. friend the leader of the opposition that I would have to communicate with His Excellency the Governor General before making any statement. This I have done. The information I have to convey to the House is that the despatch which came from the Colonial Office was a secret despatch, which we have not the right to lay upon the Table. His Excellency has communicated with the Colonial Office asking for permission, and no answer has been received.
speakername: The PRIME MINISTER (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier).

speechtext:
I would like to call the attention of the act-

ing Minister of Railways (Hon. Mr. Fielding) to tFe necessity of furnishing the House either to-day or on Monday with all possible information that is in the department in reference to surveys that were made for a contemplated railway at the time when the Canadian Pacific was building, from Lake Temiscamingue north of the height of land, north of Lake Nepigon towards Lake Winnipeg. speakername: The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Hon. W. S. Fielding).

speechtext: I can give the names of the engineers who have charge of the different surveys. There can be no doubt about it. The reports must be there.
All these reports, I think, were published at the time, and are to be found in the library. But I understood the hon. gentleman to say that there was something later.

No ; they are not published. They are reports made for the purpose of an alternative route for the Canadian '[DOT] Pacific Railway. The surveys were made under the direction of Sir Sandford Fleming (then Mr. Sanford Fleming), who was then the deputy head of the department.

I think that what my hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Haggart) refers to will be found in the different reports of the department that are on file in the library. I understand he has reference to some that were not published. I will make further inquiry about the matter.

House went into committee to consider the following proposed resolution :
That it is expedient to enact as follows:-
1.	The Governor in Council may authorize the payment of the following sums, in the respective fiscal years mentioned, for the purpose of assisting in establishing and maintaining an independent and efficient service of telegraphic news from Great Britain, for publication in the Canadian press :-

(a.) For the fiscal year 1903-4, a sum not exceeding fifteen thousand dollars, or at the rate of fifteen thousand dollars per annum for any period less than a year.
(b. )* For the fiscal year 1904-5, a sum not exceeding fifteen thousand dollars.
(c.) For the fiscal year 1905-6, a sum not exceeding fifteen thousand dollars.
(d.) For the fiscal year 1906-7, a sum not exceeding ten thousand dollars.
(e.) For the fiscal year 1907-8, a sum not exceeding five thousand dollars.
2.	The said sums may be paid at such times and in such manner as the Minister of Finance may determine, to any association or committee representing the proprietors of such newspapers as may associate themselves for the purpose of establishing and maintaining such service.
Provided, however, that no payment shall be made under authority of this Act until the Minister of Finance shall have satisfied himself that the benefits of the service are open, on fair and reasonable terms to all newspapers published in Canada; and that not less than one-half the cost of establishing and maintaining such service is paid by the proprietors of the newspapers participating in the benefits thereof.
3.	The Governor in Council may make regulations for carrying out the purposes of this Act.-The Minister of Finance.

The resolution which is before the committee, as will be seen, has reference to the granting of a sum of public money to assist in making a better cable service for the benefit of the Canadian press and, through the Canadian press, for fhe benefit of the Canadian people. I am sure that members of the committee will agree with me when I say that the manner in which our Canadian press is served with cable news from Europe, except as respects a few special despatches which they are receiving, and which are unobjectionable, is eminently unsatisfactory. I am sure that every hon. member when reading in the public press the report of something of imperial concern which has been before the British House of Commons, or in some way has engaged the attention of the people, has had reason to feel aggrieved at the tone and temper of the whole report. This arises from the fact that our Canadian newspapers -though I am glad to say they are making gratifying progress, and are making an excellent place in the journalistic world-are not, many of them, endowed sufficiently with wealth to be able to establish an independent cable service. Some two or three of the more enterprising have recently obtained special cable reports of their own, but the majority are still obliged to use the reports received by way of the United States and prepared chiefly for the United States people1. The consequence is that many things that are of interest to us in Canada are not reported at all, and many that are reported are coloured in a way that is far from agreeable to us. Several years ago I was so impressed with this fact that I asked the consent of my colleagues to make

a proposition to parliament for a public grant to assist a movement of tbis kind toward the establishing of a better service for the Canadian press. X thought then, as I think now, that the service should not be entirely supported by government, but that the newspapers themselves should bear a proper share of the expense. I had negotiations with a number of gentlemen connected with the Canadian press, in the hope that I might then be able to prepare a scheme of this character, but, as it involved a considerable outlay by the Canadian newspapers, they were not prepared at the time to respond to the suggestions we made. The proposition received their sympathy, but the financial part imposed 'too serious a burden upon the newspaper proprietors, and, for the time being, the movement was not successful.
Quite recently however some gentleman connected with the press who have been aware that the government entertained such an idea in time jiast, have approached us again and asked if we would still be disposed to carry out what was then in our minds, and I have been glad to be able to assure them on behalf of the government that if they were prepared to form an organization for giving an efficient service to the Canadian press and bear a reasonable proportion of the expense, we would be glad to make a contribution to the system. A committee composed of representatives of the press, irrespective of political parties, came here some time ago and stated that if we would agree to give a moderate degree of assistance they would themselves undertake to raise a considerable sum of money. We have come to the conclusion to ask the House to approve of the grant of the sums which we have mentioned in these resolutions $15,000 for the first, second and third years, $10,000 for the fourth year, and $5,000 for the fifth year. We are assuming that the press will develop considerably, and that while at the beginning they cannot aid as much as we would like them to do, and they would like to do for themselves, we expect that after several years they will be able to gather in the subscriptions of a larger number of newspapers and be able to carry on the service effectively after the expiration of the five years. We leave the scheme largely to the newspapers. The government do not assume to exercise any control over it. We propose to deal,' as the resolution says, with an association or committee representing the press generally.
speakername: The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Hon. W. S. Fielding).

speechtext: Have they not outlined any scheme yet ?	[DOT]

Not further than this, that we have intimated to them that for a time at least they should undertake to provide a service, to employ correspondents, to pay for cable bills and do all that is necessary to create an efficient service, and they have agreed to secure the co-operation of as many newspapers in
Canada as are able to contract for the service. The newspapers in the large cities will have to pay a much larger amount than the newspapers in the smaller centres, although all will receive the service alike ; those in the large communities; will have to pay more, those in the smaller communities will pay less, though they all get the same news. We leave the gentlemen of the press to work out all the details for themselves. The conditions which we impose are, first, that they raise and spend for the service at least as much money as the government does. The second condition is that they must hold the service open to every newspaper in Canada on fair and reasonable terms ; and unless they can show us that everybody in Canada who wants to contract has all the privileges which this scheme offers them they are not entitled to receive the money. We leave the working out of the details entirely to the newspaper people, and we accept the assurance which the representatives that the leading papers have given us that they will work it out on an entirely non-partisan basis, and with the co-operation of the press generally throughout the Dominion.
Mr. BORDEN" (Halifax.) I heartily and cordially support the proposal of the Minister of Finance In this regard. I am satisfied that the people of this country have not had fair play in the way of getting news from England during the past, and on the other hand the people of England perhaps have not been any better supplied with Canadian news. We have had to get a great deal of our news through sources which are coloured, not certainly from a Canadian or an English standpoint. While I am not disposed to make any reflection in that direction, nevertheless I feel satisfied from what information I have obtained, and that I have had placed before me in connection with this very matter, that certain events of great public consequence in the mother country have sometimes come to us with a certain colour which is not desirable either in the interest of the empire or in the interest of Canada. If it is possible by aid of this kind to ensure that the press of Canada shall have fair and accurate reports of events of public importance in the mother country, and that the people of the mother country shall have accurate and adequate means of knowing what is being done and published in Canada, I think a great service will be rendered to the country. I do not know how it is in Great Britain at the present time, I have not had the pleasure of visiting that country for six or seven years ; but I know that during my previous visits I have often been intensely disappointed, I might even use a stronger word, at the very great dearth of news of my country that appeared in the English papers. In many of them there was not a word regarding Canada for a considerable time, and in the more import-

ant journals only a line or two and perhaps not that. If this grant will contribute to any better result, and I have every reason to believe that it will, I think there is no person in this country who would not heartily join in supporting the proposition of my hon. friend the Minister of Finance.

Some time, either in the month of June or July, I attended a meeting of gentlemen connected with this project in the city of Montreal. At that time they did not appear to have any clearly defined scheme in their minds, I hope it has been made clearer since. At the meeting to which I allude there were, besides newspaper men, some business men. Similar meetings I understand had been held in Toronto and elsewhere. If I understood what was in their minds, their idea was to form a kind of a joint stock company to-, gether and send news. It was in my capa-citj' of a newspaper man that I was invited to attend the meeting ; there were only a few newspaper men present for the city of Montreal. I would like to know from the Minister of Finance on what conditions he proposes to pay that pretty large sum of money. So far as I understood the idea of the newspaper men, it was to act in opposition to the existing cable, or at any rate to the existing state of affairs. The object was not very clear, and that is the reason why I inquire. Let me say before taking my seat that, being no more Minister of Public Works, I am more free to fight for the rights of my former department. I think my hon. friend the Minister of Finance is invading the realm of the minister of telegraph. If it were in my days I would kick. I make that remark in a very friendly spirit, but all the same I claim that when a department has direct charge of business-like telegraphs the hon. Minister of Finance should at least agree that the minister of telegraphs should make a report jointly with him. That is only fair. I have no personal ends to serve and I make these observations in all friendship.

In regard to the statement of my hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Tarte) that it is an invasion of the Public Works Department, I may say that it is not an invasion of any department for the Minister of Finance to provide the money. I have never found that any department had the least objection to the Minister of Finance providing money. 1 am not clear that any particular department has charge of this business, but 1 may say that when the Minister of Public Works required money for the Harbour Commissioners of Montreal, a matter coming within the purview of his department, as far as expenditure is concerned, it was always the Minister of Finance who brought up the appropriation and gave him the money, so that we are simply following the same rule in this case as in Mr. BORDEN (Halifax).
other cases. My hon. friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden, Halifax), whose commendation and co-operation I am glad to welcome, I am afraid connected this resolution with a matter which is a little beyond its scope when he suggested that we might make provision not only for news coming from Great Britain, but also for a supply of news from Canada to Great Britain. That is very desirable indeed.
This scheme may work out in that way.

Yes, this scheme may lead to it. You have to make arrangements with the English papers to publish your news and this is not a matter that can be directed from this side of the Atlantic. If we could do anything to induce English papers to give more prominence to Canadian affairs it would be well worth our pains to attempt to do something in that direction. I am glad to know that of late years there has been a vastly increased interest taken in colonial affairs, and particularly in Canadian affairs, and we find that the English newspapers are to-day disposed to publish much more matter from Canada than formerly. They have a number of special correspondents in Ottawa. I have had the pleasure of meeting three of four gentlemen representing the British press within a few days who have come out to visit Canada, not only those with the British press party, but others who have come out individually. I think if anything could be done to arouse an increased interest in London, and to bring about the publication of Canadian events in the British papers it would be very desirable.
Am I correct in understanding that this cable service will be quite independent of the American lines V
Yes.
What will be the cost per word for these despatches, and what number of words will be received per day during the year for that amount ?

I am afraid I cannot give the hon. gentleman that information. When we say it will be independent of the American lines, what we mean is that there will be a Canadian correspondent in London and he will do work entirely for the Canadian service, and that will give us a purely Canadian service. We do not make any condition hs to what particular cable the news must come over. As to rates, I have no reason to suppose that the rates will be any lower than they now are. Just what number of words this will give each day is a point that I could hardly undertake to speak upon.
What are the rates now?
The press rate is 12i cents per word, or halt the ordinary commercial rate. The commercial rate is 25 cents a word, and the press rate is 12J cents a word.
What about utilizing the Marconi system ?

I have no doubt they will, and if they do they will get the benefit of the rates for which we have stipulated. On that point we have not very much information as to the recent movements of the Marconi system. A representative of the company was here recently, he came to see me and he said that while they had suffered some difficulties aud delays, he felt satisfied that within a very little time they would be able to carry out all they had undertaken.

As a matter of fact is there not another company that has made some better progress than the Marconi company ? I have noticed some tests between the two companies in the United States, the Deforest Company and the Marconi Company, and I observed that on two recent occasions messages transmitted by the instruments of the Marconi Company have been tapped by another company? One of these occasions was only a day or two ago.

There is another company which has been making very great progress. As to the relative merits of the two systems, I would not be in a position to offer any opinion. The Marconi system is admittedly successful for short distances as the Deforest system is. As to long distances, I would not say anything as to their relative merits, but they are both successful as to short distances. At present the Deforest company has not attempted ocean telegraphy, but they have it in contemplation, and they believe that they can carry it out more successfully than the Marconi Company. They have made some proposals to the departments looking to the adoption of the Deforest system in the Canadian government service.

I should think it would be extremely desirable for the government to make sure as to the success of either system before spending any more money in connection with it. It seemed to me extremely inconsistent that last year we should be making a grant of money in favour of the Marconi Company, and at the same time building cable lines in localities which should be served by this company if this invention is going to amount to anything. I do not know anything of the relative merits of the two systems, but I think that possibly the hon. Minister of Finance may be able to tell us whether or not the Marconi system across the Atlantic is an assured success.

No, it is not a commercial success yet. I understand, however, that they are sending messages from this side to England. The representative of the company who called on me, in answer to my question as to that, said that they were prepared to transmit any message which I might give him to any of 'my friends or acquaintances in London, but that they could not undertake to bring the return message, because the power of their station in England is not as great as the power of their station in Cape Breton. That was the reason given.
It is a lop-sided system.

Well, it takes two parties to make a contract like that. I do not regret the step that we have taken in assisting the Marconi system. It is a great invention, and I think Canada obtained a little kudos for holding out her hands and assisting these people to come to Canada, and if the Marconi system should prove to be a great success in the future the government of Canada will always in the history of that invention be credited with having been the first government in the world to give it a friendly hand.
It seems to me, from the calculation that I have made, that they would not get a very big service for the amount of money that is proposed to be given.
They have to give an equal amount of money.

That would make it $30,000. If you take $30,000 and divide that by eight, which would practically give the rate per word, then divide the result by 305, the number of days in the year, you would find that the number of words that you would get would not be very many. Then you would have to deduct also from that the cost of delivery and other incidental expenses in connection with it; so that you would not get a very good service for the amount of money, unless there is some special arrangement whereby there will be a reduction in the rate that we are paying to-day.

I am afraid I will have to give away some of the family^ secrets. My hon. friend (Mr. Sproule) is too confiding when he assumes [DOT]that every word he reads in these cable despatches in the newspapers has been cabled from the other side. I have no doubt that there is an impression amongst many excellent people, when they read these long columns of cable despatches that every word came from England exactly as it appears, at the rate of sixpence per word. The fact is, that manv of these words are never cabled from England at all. These cablegrams are skeletonized, and a clever journalist can,

with the exercise of his intelligence and his experience, fill out that paragraph, save a good deal of money, and give the people an intelligent service.
That is the practice on the other side.

It is a world-wide practice in the field of journalism, and it is a legitimate practice in the hands of capable and responsible men. If you are giving the exact words of a man or a quotation from a document, of course that must be given exactly; but for the general purpose of giving news you can fill in your skeleton cable and you can do it quite legitimately.
Without destroying the sense or warping the meaning?
Certainly.
The hon. member for Grey (Mr. Sproule) is so seldom on bis feet that I have no objection to being called to order by you, Mr. Chairman, in order that I should give the floor to him.
Hear, hear.

As one of those who happened to be present when the delegation of newspaper men waited on the Finance Minister, I wish to say a word or two on this matter. The representations then made to the Finance Minister and made to myself in private conversation afterwards, were that the representatives of the press intended by this method to get an entirely uncoloured news-service so far as English cable news is concerned. My hon. friend the leader of the oposition, as stated by the Finance Minister, is evidently under a wrong impression as to the nature of this service. I would myself be glad if it were possible to have in the English newspapers a good summary of Canadian news, which apparently we have not at the present time. However the object of the newspaper men who waited on the Finance .uintster as representing the various leading papers of the country of both sides of politics, was that they might be able to obtain a much better and more complete cable service than they have at the present time. I do not know what information the late Minister of Public Works (Hon. Mr. Tarte) has over and beyond what he has stated to the House, but so far as the representations made to the Finance Minister are concerned, there was no idea or intention that there should be the establishment of an independent cable service at all. The simple idea was to procure through uncoloured channels information that would be of advantage and benefit to the people of. Canada. There is also this fact to be borne in mind-as criticism is offered by the member for East Grey -that the amount that was promised by the Finance Minister is the amount that was

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: practically asked for by the gentlemen representing the newspapers. They evidently had made some estimate as to the annual expense that would be involved, and they were perfectly satisfied with the conditional assurance of the Finance Minister that assistance of the nature now proposed should he granted. They realized that this would give to them a satisfactory news-service. Anybody who had had any experience with newspapers knows perfectly well that telegraph tolls as a rule are pretty heavy, and the newspapers do not get any more cable news than is absolutely necessary because of the great expense. Under the anticipated condition of affairs, they will have an everyday cable service that will be more satisfactory to newspaper readers and to the people of Canada generally. I understood from the remarks of the deputation that they intended taking in a number of the journals throughout the country as co-partners in this scheme. Of course, newspapers are subjected to what no other business is subject to, in that there is more or less stealing carried on by the papers that come out later than the others, and consequently no help can be obtained from some newspapers for this scheme. However, it was understood that a number of the papers joining in this organization were willing to bear their .share of this expense in connection wth the proposal as announced by the Minister of Finance. It seems to me that the proposal will meet with the cordial approval of the entire House. It is one of the few questions upon which we can all agree, and I am satisfied that it will prove a decided advantage to Canadian newspapers. If the result should be to lead to the publication of fuller and better Canadian news in the British newspapers. we will have accomplished a great deal of good for Canada by voting this money.

I feel deeply grateful to the member for Huron (Mr. Holmes) for the gratuitous information he has given to the member for East Grey, and also for the additional information he has given us as to the proclivity of the newspapermen for stealing their news.
That is only some of them.

The small press, he says.
I assume that those who acquire the habit of stealing ballots could as well steal their press despatches, and therefore it would not be much out of place for them to do so. I still believe that this scheme is not universally regarded by the press of the country as a satisfactory arrangement. I am told that the Montreal Gazette is not of the opinion that it is going to be an unqualified success, and for reasons which I need not wait to explain at the present time.
I am not opposed to the proposition because I think the principle is good. I hare al-

ways regarded it as an unfortunate thing that our news from England comes through a source that so warps it, that it is of little value to us, and does not do justice to the country or to those with whom the information originates. It is very desirable, if it be possible to attain it, that whatever news we do get shall not be coloured by the fruitful imagination of journalists, but that we should get in substance the same information that was given at the other end of the wire. That is a matter of great importance to the country, and as for news going to England, I assume that it is not so liable to misrepresentation as the news coming from England to Canada. If this succeeds in getting us correct information in cable despatches, the money, in my judgment, will be well spent.

Every one in this House knows perfectly well that when the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) addresses the House, he only speaks on subjects that he is familiar with, and hence his reference to ballot stealing must be based on personal experience.
*Some hon. MEMBERS. Hear, hear.
I am not on record as having any experience in that line like my hon. friend.

As a member of the newspaper fraternity, I believe I can express the opinion prevailing in the province of Quebec, when I congratulate the government on this new departure. It is certainly a sign of the times, and I hope the benefits of the proposal will be lasting for the Canadian press and for the Canadian people. The scheme is so good a one that I am sorry it has been limited in its operation to Great Britain. We have in Canada more than a million and a half of Canadian citizens who take a very deep interest in what goes on in France. Successive governments have made praiseworthy efforts to renew our commercial relations with France; the Conservative government brought about a treaty with France and the present government is following up the efforts which were made in that direction in the past. I trust, therefore, that the government will not overlook the importance of having a branch of this cable service extended to Paris. London, of course, is the centre of the English world, as Paris is the centre for continental news, and it is in the interest of Canada that certain things which happen in 'France: should be reported to the Canadian press from Paris itself, and not receive a colouring in London, as unfortunately has happened when some little friction has sprung up. While I commend the effort that is now being made, I hope that the government will see that this Canadian Press Association will have an agency established In Paris, not only for French news, but for
continental news generally. No Canadian now goes to Europe without going to Paris, and no trip to Europe is complete without a visit to Paris. If we wish to extend our commercial and social relations with Europe, I believe that we should have a representative of the Canadian press in Paris, and that Canadian news should be sent to Paris, which is the centre of distribution for the whole continent.

I am glad to be able to assure my hon. friend (Mr. Marcil) that the matter which he has spoken of has not escaped our attention. When I was discussing the subject with the gentlemen of the press who called on me, I suggested to them that it might be desirable that we should take into consideration the needs of the French press, and I asked them to communicate with some of the French newspapers and ascertain to what extent they desire communication with Paris. I anticipated that it might be necessary to stipulate that there should be an agency in Paris, but I am informed, and though my information is at second-hand, I think it is correct, that the leading French papers take the view that while they .were desirous of having occasional telegrams from Paris, when something of importance occurred, they did not think there was enough news of interest to Canada to require a regular correspondent to be established there in the same sense as in London. I anticipate, however, that the committee will see that a connection is made with Paris for getting French news, and supplying as much of that to the French newspapers as they are desirous of having. I can assure the hon. gentleman that the matter has been considered, the committee has been in communication with the proprietors of some of the French newspapers, and I am assured that they are in sympathy with the movement in its present shape.

Have the committee or the gentlemen who are to compose the proposed association had under consideration at all the subject of supplying Canadian news to the English press ? I regard it as very important that the news which is distributed throughout the United Kingdom with regard to Canada should go as much as possible direct from Canada, and I believe that is not the case at the present time to a very great extent, except with the great journals;

Though it is not the case to as large an extent as we could wish, it is the case to a much larger extent titan ever before. There are two well known press agencies in England, the Reuter and the Exchange Telegram Company, both of which have correspondents at Ottawa; and when a despatch goes to either of these agencies, it is distributed to a large number of newspapers. In addition to that, several papers have

their special correspondents, who, though they do not send daily telegrams, do send telegrams when anything of importance occurs. While X realize that this service is much better than it was in former years, it is not yet all that we desire, and I shall be glad if this association can be the means of improving it. The newspaper men of Canada represent to me that while they can enter into an agreement for news to be printed in the Canadian press, they have no guarantee that any news they might send to England would be printed in the English newspapers if it were sent. So that I do not think that at the present time we are able to do in that respect what my hon. friend and myself both desire. I hope the effect of this arrangement will be to help the other end of the service, and that, ere long, we shall have a better service on both sides than we have at present.
Resolutions reported, read the first and the second time, and agreed to.
The MINISTER OP FINANCE moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 240) to assist in establishing and maintaining an independent and efficient service of telegraphic news from Great Britain for publication in the Canadian press.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

The PRIME MINISTER (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier) moved second reading of Bill (No. 155) respecting the jurisdiction of the Exchequer Court as to railway debts. He said :	This is a Bill which has been
placed on the government orders, but which has been introduced into the House by my hon. friend from St. John and Iberville (Mr. Demers).	.

speakeroldname: Mr. L. P. DEMERS (St. John and Iberville).
speechtext: In 1890 an Act respecting the jurisdiction of the Exchequer Court as to railway debts was enacted as chapter 44. By this Act leave was given to the mortgagees, creditors or holders of debentures against a railway to obtain from the Exchequer Court a decree of sale of the railway. Since that time it has been discovered that there were other parties to whom no leave was given. These are the ordinary creditors and the public at large. It is proposed by this Bill to give relief to these parties. It is a well-known fact that many of our railroads are not operated during certain parts of the year, and though the public at large suffer, this government has not been able to afford a proper remedy. It is proposed by this Act to permit the Minister of Railways and Canals when a railway is insolvent to apply to the Exchequer Court for an order of sale and for the appointment of a receiver.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext:
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the second time, and House went into committee thereon.
On section 1,
Is it intended by this Bill to take away any of the jurisdiction which a provincial court might exercise so far as a railway wholly situated in a province is concerned ?
The purpose of the Act is not to take away the jurisdiction of provincial courts. It is in accordance with what was in the Act of 1899.

We have railways in Nova Scotia, which are subject to the legislative authority of the parliament of Canada, but which are wholly in the province of Nova Scotia. Is it intended by this Bill to vest exclusive jurisdiction over such railways in the Exchequer Court? I do not know that there are any words in the Bill which necessarily would lead to that interpretation, but, some question might be raised ; and if it is not intended to deprive provincial courts of any jurisdiction they have at present, it would be better to state so specifically. I might bring to the attention of my hon. friend from St. John and Iberville the use of the word ' insolvent ' in subsection (a). Has he defined that word anywhere in the Bill ?

Yes, in section 5. As I have already stated, clause 1 of the Bill, defining the railways over which the Exchequer Court of Canada shall have jurisdiction, is taken verbatim from the statutes of 1899, chapter 44.
This section simply re-enacts that ?

No, it goes further. While the same railways fall under the jurisdiction of the Exchequer Court, as are defined in chapter 44 of the statutes of 1899, the jurisdiction of the Exchequer Court is extended beyond that Act to ordinary creditors and to roads not operated.

This legislation is rendered absolutely imperative by

the judgment of the Privy Council in Grey vs. the Manitoba and North-western. The Privy Council held that no provincial court has jurisdiction to deal with a railway as an entity, which exceeds beyond the limits of the particular province in question, so that in order to have such a railway sold, it is necessary to vest some federal court with jurisdiction over it. As regards a railway entirely within the limits of a province but which is under federal jurisdiction, owing to its having been declared a work for the general utility of Canada, I cannot see any good reason why a provincial court should not have jurisdiction to deal with it. It is an immovable and entirely within the limits of the province.

I agree absolutely with my hon. friend that, as regards a railway which extends beyond the limits of a province, we must confer jurisdiction on the Exchequer Court. But there is a question as to those wholly within, although as the hon. member for St. John and Iberville points out, he has used exactly the same language in that regard as is to be found in the Act of 1899. We have had no difficulty in Nova Scotia about working out these matters in respect of a railway wholly within that ^province. My hon. friend from Annapolis knows that our courts have dealt with these matters without any difficulty whatever, and it seems to me that it would be more convenient to deal with them in the province where our courts are readily accessible and not have to go to Ottawa for the issue of process and the many interlocutory applications necessary in litigation of that kind. Of course, in so far as this Bill proposes to confer upon the Exchequer Court powers which are not exercisable by any provincial court, and which are in the public interest, you migh leave it as it is with respect to interprovincial railways; but in the ease of a railway situated wholly within the province, it would be better to have those powers exercised by the highest court of the province. Has my hon. friend from St. John considered that point in his Bill ?

I would be very sorry indeed to see any of the powers of our provincial courts taken away. I do not think that the wording of this section deprives them of any jurisdiction. It only confers jurisdiction on the Exchequer Court in eases where it is not vested in a provincial court. If there be any doubt, it would be well to add a clause providing that this Bill shall not detract from any jurisdiction now vested in our provincial courts.

There is a little more in it upon which I would be very glad to know the opinions of members of the bar throughout' the House. This Bill does confer powers upon the Exchequer Court which are not at present exercisable by provincial courts. But in respect of a railway situated
wholly within a province, is it better to confer those powers upon the Exchequer Court or the provincial court of the highest jurisdiction ? At this moment there is no good reason why those powers should not be exercised by the highest court in the province in respect of a railway wholly situated within that province.
The Bill only concerns railways over which the Privy Council has decided that the provincial courts have no jurisdiction.

I agree that the Exchequer Court is a proper tribunal to have jurisdiction in respect of any railway extending through more than one province. But why should not the provincial court of the highest jurisdiction exercise those powers in respect of a railway situated within a province ? I take, for example, the Dominion Atlantic Railway, or the Nova Scotia Central Railway, which are entirely within the province of Nova Scotia. Suppose you want to exercise the powers here conferred upon the Minister of Railways and Canals or upon any creditor, to sue for a decree against such a railway because it has become insolvent, or has for more than ten days failed to efficiently continue the working or operating of such railway, why should you not have the decree made by the Supreme Court of Nova Scotia instead of by the Exchequer Court ?
It seems to me that the suggestion of the leader of the opposition is a good one.

If it were decided to carry out the suggestion of the hon. leader of the opposition, all that would be required would be to strike out the words ' or as regards any railway otherwise subject to the legislative authority of the parliament of Canada.' This would restrict the jurisdiction to those railways not wholly within one province. But the question arises as to whether it is or is not wise to give the federal court which is under our control absolute jurisdiction in all matters connected with railways that are under federal authority. It seems to me that this would be desirable rather than to follow the suggestion of the leader of the opposition. There is no reason why a railway that is under federal jurisdiction, even if it is wholly within the limits of one province, should not be made subject to the jurisdiction of the Exchequer Court, the same as with a railway extending beyond the limits of one province. It seems to me it would be better to make uniform legislation. That would not exclude the concurrent jurisdiction of the courts of the province in dealing with those railways that are situated wholly within the province. My hon. friend will remember the decision in" the case of Redfieid vs. Corporation of Wickham, where the Privy Council held that

a provincial court had a right to sell a railway. I will read from that decision
They do not suggest that, according to the policy of Canadian law a statutory railway undertaking can be disintegrated by piecemeal sales at the instance of judgment creditors or incumbrances; but they clearly show

And this is the important part

-ittoait the Dominion parliament has recognized the rule that a railway or a section of railway may, as an integer, be taken in execution, and sold, like other immeubles, in ordinary course of law. They justify the statement of Chief Justice Dorion, in the present case, that 'it is now well settled by the jurisprudence prevailing in this country, and recognized by the Act 46 Vic. c. 43, that a railway can be seized and sold for the debts of the company who owns such a railway.
That was a railway which came within the operation of our Dominion Act, but, being entirely situated within the limits of the province of Quebec, it was held that the provincial courts had jurisdiction, and the railway could be taken in execution and disposed of by the sheriff absolutely in the same way as any other property.

I agree with everything that the Minister of Justice (Hon. Mr. Fitzpatrick) has said with regard to the operation of the law. The old rule, of course, was that, in respect to a railway you ' could not cut down the trees, but only take the fruit '-you could put a receiver in charge and use the revenue to pay a judgment creditor.
That, however, never prevailed on this side of the water.

That prevailed in England. And they put it on the ground of public policy-that a railway was intended to be a public service, and you could not interfere with the service at the instance of the creditors, but you could give him relief by giving him the rents and tolls through a receiver. I do not knoW whether I clearly apprehended the reason on account of which the Minister of Justice said that these powers should be conferred on the federal court. Would he be good enough to repeat briefly the reason that he gave in that regard ? I suggested that, in the case of a railway wholly within one province, it would he more convenient to confer the jurisdiction upon a provincial court. The hon. gentleman made some answer to that.

I do not thiuk I answered that. No doubt, it would be convenient in one way to have the court of the province continue exercising its jurisdiction. But I said that we conferred jurisdiction upon the Exchequer Court in these cases to deal with railways under federal jurisdiction, whether they were under our jurisdiction because they have been declared to be works for the general advant-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: age of Canada, or because they connected with certain railways mentioned in the Railway Act, or because they extended beyond the limits of one province; and it seemed to me better, for the uniformity of legislation, that we should give federal jurisdiction over all. This could be done without interfering with the existing jurisdiction In the provincial courts with respect to those railways which though federal in their character, are situated entirely within the limits of one province, and the suggestion as to that point I am ready to agree to.

But the hon. minister will see that you do not secure uniformity even if you do adopt his suggestion, for the provincial courts will still have power to sell a railway at the instance of the creditor under the powers which are vested in it apart from any statute. Is there any reason why you should not give to that court the additional powers that are created by this statute ? In one sense it would be more uniform to give the powers to the Exchequer Court, but we do not attempt uniformity of that kind in other things. With respect to insolvency we confer jurisdiction upon the provincial courts ; even in the case of the elections to this parliament, we confer jurisdiction on provincial courts. This is a matter of some importance to provinces situated at a long distance from this capital, the place where the Exchequer Court has . its headquarters.
For example, take the province of British; Columbia, or of Prince Edward Island, or of Nova Scotia, it is a very difficult thing for them to transact business in the Exchequer Court on account of the long distance. In cases of this kind you would naturally have a great deal of interlocutory business, there is no local judge, and you may have to have the business transacted in Ottawa. It might be a very desirable thing that the local solicitor or counsel should be present at motions and proceedings of that kind. Unless you can give some strong reason for restricting jurisdiction to the Exchequer Court, it would seem to me to be the wiser course to let the provincial courts within the province deal with these matters so far as railways wholly situated within the province are concerned. That would be my own view, though I realize that there may be some reason for the opposite view. It is not a matter I am pressing very vigorously.

I would like the hon. gentleman to say whether he can see any objection to giving concurrent jurisdiction to the provincial court and the Exchequer Court. The provincial court is now undoubtedly vested with jurisdiction to deal with these particular railways, and is there any difficulty or any objection to granting to the Exchequer Court jurisdiction also over these railways, so that it might

be optional with a creditor to select his own court ?

Speaking offhand, I do not see any objection to that. My hon. friend suggests that all statutory powers which are created by this proposed Bill are to be Conferred upon provincial courts concurrently with the Exchequer Court, so far as railways only situated within the province are concerned.
Mr. WADE; Is it not a fact that at the present time provincial courts have complete jurisdiction over railways, no matter whether they are railways declared to be for the general advantage of Canada or not, and no matter whether they are entirely situated within the province ?
That is right.
It has no power to order the sale of a railway that extends beyond the province. Our provincial courts have not that power.
I am only saying that there are certain powers which are statutory powers and are not vested at the present time in the provincial courts because they are creatures of this statute.
What power ?

The power, for example, to sell a railway because the company has failed to work it for ten days. I wish to make myself clear to the hon. member for Annapolis (Mr. Wade). I mean that so far as you are creating powers here which are not at present vested in any provincial court you should vest these powers in a provincial court at least concurrently with the Exchequer Court so far as railways wholly situated within a province are concerned.

I asked whether that is not the case now. Have they not absolute power ?
Mr. BORDEN (Halifax;. I am talking about powers created by this statute, which do not exist outside this statute.
That is the very thing.

I understand the leader of the opposition to say that in this Bill, we are conferring certain specific powers upon the judge of the Exchequer Court, we are -granting that court certain powers that are not now vested in it, and the leader of the opposition suggests that we should give to the judges in the provincial courts these same powers with respect to this particular class of railway that we are vesting in the Exchequer Court.
Exactly.

It is suggested to me by a layman that there might
be a difficulty in giving the courts concurrent jurisdiction. You may have one creditor going to the local court for the purpose of having the railway brought to sale, and another creditor going to the Exchequer Court. There might be a conflict of jurisdiction between the two courts. There does appear to be something in that. We will have to guard against that.

You can easily guard against that. A court in which a second action is taken always stays proceedings until the first action is determined. There are cases where an action is taken in two different courts each having jurisdiction. For example, an action might be brought in the province of New Brunswick and another in Nova Scotia, both going on at the same time, one brought before the other. The usual course is that the court in which the second action is brought stays proceedings until the first action has been determined. That is also the rule which has been acted upon in England within a very few years past, and acted upon in the Supreme Court of Nova Scotia. Not long ago a similar case was decided in England, I forget the name of it, perhaps the Minister of Justice is familiar with it-a case where an action had been brought in either a French or an Italian court, and the action was also brought in England during the pendency of that foreign action. The English court, if my memory serves me correctly, simply stayed proceedings until the foreign action had been determined, then they gave the judgment in accordance with the decision which had been arrived at in the foreign court. There would be no difficulty on that score.

I would ask the promoter of this Bill this question. Suppose there is an action brought in the province of Quebec by a creditor of a railway company before the Exchequer Court, and there is a sale ordered of the property. Is that sale adjudicated by a provincial court in the province of Quebec, that is, does the provincial court transfer the property absolutely, and are the proceeds received from the sale of the property distributed by the court among the different creditors according to their rank ? Would the judgment of the Exchequer Court have two different effects in different provinces ? Iii the xwovince of Ontario it would be only a sale of the franchise, in the province of Quebec it would be an absolute disposition of the property. Now suppose a party holds bonds under a Dominion statute, or securities, or perhaps a mortgage, on a judgment obtained before the Exchequer Court against a Dominion railway which has a Dominion charter in the province of Quebec ; now if this property is disposed of as the court in the province of Quebec has a right to dispose of it, that is making an absolute

sale, that would not be the case if he held securities.

I understand that the suggestion of the hon. leader of the opposition would meet that difficulty, because the suggestion of the hon. gentleman was that we should confer upon the provincial court the same powers that we confer upon the Exchequer Court so that the powers which could be exercised by the courts in each of the provinces would be the same as those which are exercised by the Exchequer Court. The difficulty of tlie hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Haggart) would be met by the suggestion of the hon. leader of the opposition.
Yes.

The security from a company which has a Dominion charter which the holder of a mortgage has is the franchise of the company which can be sold if the debts of the company are not paid, but if you get judgment in the Exchequer Court here against a company in the province of Quebec you can sell the property absolutely although the property might only bring one-fifth of the value of these prior securities should the court order. There is no sale in Quebec that is not an absolute transfer of the property. Then, the courts act as the receiver and distributes the money received for the property according to the rank of the security.

If a company were authorized, in Ontario for instance, to give a mortgage on its franchise, and covering not only its franchise, but its rolling stock, permanent way and buildings, you surely could sell these on foreclosure proceedings ?
Yes, but you could not by an ordinary execution. You could only sell the franchise or the right to run the road.
Subject to the claim of the mortgagee.

That was the law, but in 1899 this parliament decreed that the Exchequer Court could sell the railway. The Act was passed in 1899 permitting the Exchequer Court to sell the property, but I do not see anything in the Railway Act authorizing the sale of the franchise.

I think I am compelled to agree with the hon. member for Lanark (Hon. Mr. Haggart) in regard to this question. We have to be a little cautious as to how we apply certain provisions that are in this proposed Bill. As far as the general jurisdiction of a railway situated exclusively in a province, although the railway may be subject to the legislative jurisdiction of Canada, is concerned, our courts have already full and complete jurisdiction over Hon. Mr. HAGGART.
them in the matter of the foreclosure of the mortgage, the sale of the road, and appointment of a receiver in connection with the property.
Not in Quebec.

Of course I cannot speak for Quebec, because I am not familiar with the law there, but it seems to me that in the province of Quebec to that extent they must have jurisdiction. I can speak with authority in regard to our own province as the matter has been thoroughly threshed out in the case which has been referred to by the hon leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden, Halifax), the English principle to which he referred was also settled in that case, and the distinction which prevails between the situation of English railways and our own was clearly defined. By the English statute law they do not permit the company to mortgage anything more than their tolls. They do not permit them to mortgage their property or their franchise, hence, the only thing you can do under the trust which they give to secure their bonds and debentures is to apply for the appointment of a receiver, operate the road under the receiver and in that way collect the tolls for the purpose of paying their debts. But, under the charters that are granted here the company not only mortgage their property, but their franchise, and you can take foreclosure proceedings in regard to all the property and the franchise of the company, and the party purchasing them will have all the powers that the company possessed in the way of operating the road. All these powers our court possesses at the present time in regard to roads which are wholly within the province and the only restriction upon its power of sale is where the road is partly in one province and partly in another. The hon. leader of the opposition has asked that they should be clothed with that jurisdiction, which this Bill proposes to give to the Exchequer Court only, an extraordinary jurisdiction to cover two classes of cases, one is where the company have not paid their debts or met their liabilities, and the other is where they have failed to operate the road. In other words, any creditor of the company may go before the Exchequer Court and proceed against the company, and ask for an order for the sale of the road, or if the road has not been in operation for ten days, any person may do the same thing. This a very large and a very extra ordinary jurisdiction which we are conferring upon the Exchequer Court, and it seems to me that it might be dangerous to give that jurisdiction to the provincial courts, because, as has been said by some one, we must look at the effeet that legislation of this kind would have upon the securities which have been issued by the company and which are held abroad. Anything that has a tendency to weaken these

securities is not wise legislation, and I think that where this extraordinary jurisdiction is sought by any person it should be before a court that has general jurisdiction, and there cannot be any hardship in taking these proceedings before the Exchequer Court. It should not be given to the provincial courts to act in the matter, especially in cases where the railway is under the legislative authority of the Dominion parliament. I do not apprehend that the provincial courts would not act just as wisely or just as carefully in the matter or not give quite as good a judgment in each case as the Exchequer Court would, but what I am looking at is the effect of this legislation upon the securities of the railway company. When it is proposed that on the motion of any party the provincial court could proceed to have the road sold, I think it would be better to have the matter remain in the hands of the Exchequer Court, because it does not weaken the jurisdiction of the provincial courts in regard to any other matters.
Mr. BORDEN (Halifax), If there is any weakening of the securities it is effected not by the court to which the jurisdiction is assigned, but by the legislation itself. If it is possible that the securities may be weakened by conferring this jurisdiction upon the provincial courts, why the same result would not be effected by conferring it upon the Exchequer Court is rather too fine a point for my intellect to grasp.
I will explain why I think so.

You could only explain it in this way :	You think one
court would exercise it wisely and that the other court would not exercise it wisely. I think the provincial courts are just as capable of exercising their judgment wisely and discreetly as the Exchequer Court. I think this power should be conferred upon the provincial courts concurrently with the Exchequer Court.

I took care to say that the provincial courts would give as wise a judgment as the Exchequer Court. I do not think there is any trouble about their judgment; and there is no doubt that they would do right ; but I do say, it would have a much more serious effect on the security if it were known that any court in a province could take this extraordinary proceeding. It would have much more serious effect on the securities than it would, if this jurisdiction could only be exercised by a central court, and that court the court of the Exchequer. I think the general public would have more confidence, that it would not be exercised hastily. I think further, that there should be some striking urgency for any proceedings to carry out the provisions of this section, and such an urgency as would make it worth the parties while to make
application to the .Exchequer Court rather than to some local court. If we make it too general it will be dangerous legislation.

What the hon. member (Mr. Wade) says goes to prove the contention of the leader of the opposition that there must be some difference between the two forums. If there is a confidence on account of going into one forum that would not obtain in going into another, it must be because one forum is deficient.
There would be this difference. In one case there is one court and one judge before whom these proceedings could be instituted ; in the other case there might be sixty judges.

That would make no difference unless you say that the sixty were inferior to the one.
Some lion. MEMBERS. Hear, hear.

I can very well understand that the Exchequer Court on account of its mode of procedure, on account of having rules that are better fitted than the rules of the Supreme Court-for example under our Judicature Act in Nova Scotia-may be a better court to wind up a railway company in that its machinery might be more operative, but, I cannot understand the other proposition. I think perhaps that this section is too broad. There are three cases in which the Minister of Railways and Canals or any creditor or a company may ask for an order to decree the sale of the railway : (1.) When the company has become insolvent;	(2.)
If for ten days it has failed to efficiently continue the working or operating of the railway, and (3.) If it has become unable so to do There might be a bridge down for example so that for ten days they would be absolutely unable to operate the railway. These words are too broad. Has the minister looked into that ?

I would suggest that this section be allowed to go through, with the understanding that before the third reading, we will consider it in the light of this discussion, the extent to which we may he able to improve the Bill.

That will be quite satisfactory.
On subsection (b).

I think there is one very strong objection to the operation of that section. It says :
Or, at the instance of a mortgagee of such railway or section, to order or decree the foreclosure of the interest of the person or company owning or entitled to such railway or such section, with the rolling stock, equipment and other accessories thereof, or the equity of redemption therein, whenever in like circumstances of default the high court of justice in England can, at the time this Act comes into force, so order or decree with resnect to mortgaged premises situate in England.

As has already been pointed out, they do not order the sale of the road ; they simply put the road into the hands of a receiver and take the tolls, and I submit that these lines should be striken out, or otherwise we will render the whole Act inoperative. I would make another suggestion in regard to this clause and the preceding clause, and that is, that the power of sale should include the power of selling the franchise as well as the railway equipment and accessories. The franchise would hardly be considered within the term ' accessories.' I presume that the mortgages in the past always covered the franchise, but we do not say in this section that we will sell the nvortaged premises ; we say we will sell the railway and the equipment and the accessories. Where you are defining, it seems to me that these are words of limitation and would exclude the franchise, unless it is expressly provided in the statute.

I wish to draw the attention of the hon. gentleman to the words of the statute. Provision is made for the sale :
Whenever in like circumstances of default the high court of Justice in England can, at the time this Act conies into force, so order or decree with respect to mortgaged premises situate in England.
Not, with respect to railways, so that we give to our Exchequer Court in dealing with this railway, the same power as the~ High Court in England with respect, not to railways, but mortgaged premises; thus avoiding the very difficulty that my hon. friend suggests.
On section 3,
What do you mean by the word ' making ' in this clause ?
If I understand it aright these are alternative powers ; they may make a sale of the road or they may appoint a receiver.
Under the direction of the court.
They are rather interlocutory powers; things to be done in the meantime pending a suit.
The clause seems somewhat involved. The word ' making ' seems to be out of place.

It seems to me that some of the functions given here to the receiver are more than what are ordinarily given to receivers. Some of them are rather the functions of a manager, and it might be well to use that term in the statute.

As used in our statutes, we know what the word *receiver' means, and I would not like to change its meaning very much. But I do not see very well what meaning can be attached to the word ' making.' The receiver Mr. WADE.
is not appointed, as a rule, for the purpose of building a railway, but for the purpose of operating a railway. I do not see the sense of the word being used here.

I think the word, as it is used here, is important, and it should be left in, because the railway might not be completed, and it would be necessary for the receiver to go on and complete it. I had some experience of that kind myself. I was the receiver of a railway for some six years. In that case the road was not completed, although it was nearly so, and it was necessary for me to obtain a special order of the court to have power to go on and complete the road, and I did so. The same thing may often be the case, and it may take months to get final order from the court to give the receiver power to complete the road, which may be necessary in the interest of all parties concerned. I think the word ' making ' should remain in the Bill.

What the hon. leader of the opposition said is, I think, correct, that this is not an Act for the building of a railway, but for the sale of a railway. If it were intended that the receiver should have power to build a railway, or a section of a railway, he might go on and wreck the property worse than it was at the time he was appointed receiver, and the consequence would be that the creditors would get nothing, and the railway might not be sold, but be kept in the hands of the receiver. This is going to be an Act which will be the foundation for the Exchequer Court dealing with railways in Canada in future ; and. in view of the very extensive building of railways in Canada, we should wisely see that nothing is put in this Act other than what would be used in the interest of the creditors and the railway itself. If a railway has to go into the hands of a receiver, the stockholders are not likely to get anything ; but if the stockholders lose, I do not want those who have advanced money on mortgage or the workmen to lose. But do not let this man who is appointed receiver go on and build the railway in sections. I think that is too much power to give to a receiver, who, as the hon. leader of the opposition said, is only an interim official appointed to keep the railway in operation and to see that the money, as it comes in, is deposited in a bank and kept. That is what I look on as a receiver, and not a person to build railways.

The word * making ' is so wide in its meaning that it would enable the receiver to extend the railway in all directions, and even to build branches. He could ruin the whole property if he were so minded.

It has been suggested to me that the word ' making ' was put there for the purpose of meeting a specific case which we have in the

province of Quebec. There are six miles of a railway to be completed to an important centre, and the word is put in to enable the receiver, if so ordered, to complete that road. The section provides that the receiver shall act under the direction of the court; and, that being the case, I do not see any great objection to the word.
The receiver is not necessarily an interim receiver. He may continue to manage the property for years.
The receiver would be an interim one, no matter how long his duty would last.
All receivers are interim in that sense.
1 think the words are clear enough. 'A receiver is appointed for the interim preservation of the property.

It is well known that in the western states a great many railways, which went into the hands of receivers because of over capitalization or because they were built where they were not needed, were operated much more successfully than those which remained in the hands of the original companies. This power being exercised, as has been pointed out by the Minister of Justice, under the constant direction and control of the court, no such difficulty as my hon. friend apprehends will be encountered in the operation of these roads. As to giving the receiver the right to complete the road under direction of the court, that may be very necessary in order to enable the road to make any profit. As regards extending the powers of the receiver, I remember distinctly that when my hon. friend from Annapolis (Wr. Wade) was receiver of the road to which he has referred he was also made the manager, and he could not have operated it as successfully ns he did if he had not been given the functions of manager ns well as those of receiver. The courts have found it necessary to appoint receivers to be managers as well, in order that they might have the powers included in both offices. If you give by this Bill to a receiver all the powers of a manager, it may be Immaterial whether you use the word ' manager,' but there may be powers which it is necessary for the official to have which are not expressly given by the statute but would be dependent on the general principles of law, and in that case unless the term manager was used in the statute these powers would not be possessed.

Does the word ' making ' used in this section serve the purpose intended by the Minister of Justice ? It seems to be rather a casual way of dealing with a pretty large subject. A matter of that kind is perhaps worth the dignity of a separate section and a somewhat more 259
elaborate provision. I would suggest that the word ' completion ' would be much better than the word ' making.'

Perhaps it would be better to allow the section to go through omitting the word ' making ' altogether and then make special provision for the completion of the road as suggested by my hon. friend.
Section, as amended, agreed to.
On section 4,
The remuneration of the receiver shall be fixed by the said court, and shall, as also shall the expenses lawfully incurred by him as receiver, including the expenses of working, operation, maintenance, renewal and institution and defence of actions aforesaid, be a debt of the company and be the first charge upon the railway, or section, and upon the rolling stock, equipment, accessories and earnings thereof.

This section
provides that the remuneration of the receiver shall be fixed by the court, but it does not provide that the other expenses sliail be approved likewise by the court. The receiver therefore would pass upon his own expenses.
In order to save time perhaps we might as well let this clause stand, and I shall endeavour to have an amendment drafted by some of the officials of my department to meet the case.
It might be as well also to have a special section drafted giving the receiver the right to complete the road.
I agree with my hon. friend.

If the power does not already exist in the Exchequer Court to make regulations as to practice, it might be as well to have a section conferring that power. The general powers of the Exchequer Court may be sufficient, but I doubt if they would cover these matters.

It has power to make rules with respect to matters now within this jurisdiction, but I think not with regard to new matters such as these.
Section allowed to stand.
On section 5,
A railway company is insolvent within the meaning of this Act. in all cases which constitute insolvency under sections 5 and 6 of the Winding Up Act, except that paragraph <g) of section 5 of that Act shall not apply to cases where possession of any railway or section thereof has been taken by trustees for bondholders under the provisions of section 94 of the Railway Act, and except further that the delay to secure or compound allowed in the case mentioned in section six of



the Winding Up Act shall be fifteen days instead of sixty.

1 would
like to draw the attention of the Minister of Justice to the case of the Atlantic and Lake Superior Railway in this connection. This road was transferred, in 1900, to trustees for the bondholders. It is, to all intents and purposes insolvent, owing a large sum of money. I would like to know whether they are exempt under this law ?

It is impossible for me to say whether the law would not be applicable to a particular case, because I am not aware of the facts. But I apprehend that the Atlantic and Lake Superior is vested in trustees under terms of mortgage.
Trustees for the bondholders ?
That would be under terms of mortgage. I think the creditors under this Act would have the right to apply for the appointment of a receiver.

To make the point clear, I would move that the following words be added at the end of section 5 :-
But such transfers to trustees shall no I exclude such railway from the provisions of the present Act.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES (Hon. R. Prefontaine).

speechtext: Suppose the bondholders got possession of the railway under the Act of 1899, and they did not pay their debts and became insolvent, what remedy would you have against them?

I would like to consider this amendment. It would be better to let this section stand.
Section allowed to stand.

Before the committee reports, I would direct the attention of the Minister of Justice, and also the attention of the hon. member for St. John and Iberville (Mr. Demers), to subsection (a) of section 1. Perhaps our attention was more particularly directed to the form of that section than to the substance of it. You will observe that under the terms of subsection (b), a creditor can have the railway sold. But still, in addition to that, it is provided in subsection (a):
At the instance of the Minister of Railways and Canals, or of any creditor of any person or company owning or operating such railway or section, to order or decree in such manner as it may prescribe, the sale of such railway or section of railway, and of all the rolling stock, equipment and other accessories thereof, whenever such company has become insolvent, or has for more than ten days failed to efficiently continue the working or operating of such railway or section or any part thereof, or has become unable so to do.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Now it seems to me that this is a pretty wide power to confer upon a creditor. If he has a lien or charge, he can enforce it. But if he has not, is there any special reason why he should be empowered to move against the company in this way. You xre giving authority to sell the entire railway in three cases, insolvency, failure to operate or inability to operate. It seems to me it would be sufficient if you conferred that power upon the Exchequer Court at the instance of the Minister of Railways and Canals. I do not think that powers of that kind ought to be invoked simply to enable a creditor to get the payment of his debt. The power might be used oppressively. I think the creditor has ample protection under subsection (b), so far as the payment is concerned.
I do not think that by the old law the ordinary creditor is protected.

The objection of my hon. friend (Mr. Demers) is that the ordinary creditor, who is without a lien or claim upon the property, is without recourse. It is not open to him to take any steps, and it is unfair that he should not have, in any of the three cases, the right to apply to court for a receiver, or exercise some recourse against the company.
In my own province the creditor would get a lien upon the reality by registration of judgment. But I suppose that is not the case in the province of Quebec.
Yes.
Has not the ordinary creditor, then, a perfect remedy ?

The leader of the opposition says that the creditor obtains a judgment against an individual, and, if the individual has property, the creditor becomes by registration a judgment creditor secured by mortgage. I have never entertained any doubt of that being the law in the province of Quebec. The creditor could take suit, register his judgment against the property, and then it becomes a mortgage. It is suggested to me that that is not possible in this case, but I must say I have never entertained any doubt that that was the law.
Assuming that that is the case, I would suggest that the ordinary creditor has very good protection under subsection (b).
If the action is against the railway company there might be some difficulty there.

There would toe no difficulty in my own province, as there is a registry office in every county through which the railway runs.
Progress reported.

Would that apply to the
chaplains ?

111 tile event of a penitentiary being established in and for the North-west Territories, the salaries of the several officers and em-

Mr. MOItltlSON. What is meant by retiring an officer to promote efficiency ? Is it supposed that if a man is found obnoxious or inefficient, he can be retired without a retiring allowance.

This section is new. My experience is that men who have been in the service of a penitentiary for a number of years get very lazy and indolent, and it would be very much to our advantage to be able to remove them and put in their places men who would be able to perform their duties more satisfactorily. In some of our penitentiaries I have been able to reduce the staff by six or seven by placing young and active men in place of those who have grown fat and lazy. It is a good tiling for the men to have the possibility of removal before their eyes, but if a man has been in the service for a number of years, I would not want to remove him without giving him some retiring allowance.

rather a mistake. A man who gets a public position asks his friends to sign, and generally they do not like to refuse. If it be in the power of the minister to insist on the bond of a guarantee company, we get rid of much difficulty and hardship.
