I desire, Sir,>
to draw attention to the conditions of the regulations which have been issued in connection with the granting of the King's medal to soldiers who served in South Africa. There were two medals given. There was the Queen's medal given to all who disembarked in South Africa before May 31st, 1902, the day when the war ended. In this connection, I may say that several contingents of the Canadian Mounted Rifles were deprived of this medal because they disembarked a few days later. There was also a second medal, the King's medal, given to those who had served for eighteen months on South African soil, or up to the 31st May, 1902, and part of whose service was after December the 1st, 1901. Complaint is made that, owing to the nature of the regulations, it is impossible for any Canadian soldier who served in a Canadian corps to' get this medal. It could not have been the intention of the imperial authorities to deprive His Majesty's Canadian subjects of the honour of obtaining this medal. About two hundred non-commissioned officers and men served in more than one Canadian contingent during the war. The first service was for twelve months, and % those who served in that contingent, if they had re-enlisted at the earliest practicable moment in another Canadian corps intended for service in the Boer War, and immediately returned to South Africa, could not have put in the length of service in the field necessary to entitle them to this medal. There are, as I have said, about two hundred non-commissioned officers and men who went from Canada in the first contingent and who, on their return, re-enlisted andj went with the second contingent. But it was impossible, owing to the length of time it takes to

reach South Africa, for any of these men to put in the full service in the field whicfi would entitle them to receive the medal. A petition has been prepared by these men asking the government to request the imperial government to modify the regulations in this respect. It certainly does seem an invidious distinction that Canadian soldiers of the King should be the only ones who served in the war who, owing to the regulations, cannot receive this medal. Australians, New Zealanders, South Africans, as well as the regular troops, have received the medal. But it is impossible for any Canadian who served in a Canadian corps to receive it. The medal is greatly coveted by those who have seen service and who would like to wear it as an honourable reminder of the services they have performed on behalf of the empire. I am sorry the hon. the Minister of Militia is not here, because I propose to read for the information of the House a copy of the memorial submitted to His Excellency the Governor General in Council, asking him to take action, so that the men who volunteered twice for service in South Africa in Canadian contingents may receive this medal.
The petition is as follows :
To His Excellency the Governor General of Canada iin Council.
The humble petition of the undersigned late non-commissioned officers and members of Canadian contingents who have served twice in South Africa, during the Boer war, 1899-1902, humbly showetih.
1.	That the present regulations for the King's medal demand eighteen months service in South Africa.
2.	That the voyage from Canada is longer than from any other colony, the double trip occupying at least four months.
3.	That under the present regulations, no Canadian can obtain the King's medal, from his service in Canadian contingents.
4.	That your petitioners, whilst few iin number, being scattered from the Atlantic to the Pacific, feel confident in addressing your Excellency that they voice -the feelings of all the non-commissioned officers and men (who your petitioners believe, number some 200). who served twice in South Africa, during the Boer war.
5.	That your petitioners therefore humbly pray that application may be made to His Gracious Majesty that the regulations for the King's medial be altered to provide that in all cases in which a man has gone twice from Canada to South Africa for the purpose of taking part in the war, fourteen months service in South Africa may be held to entitle him to receive the King's medal.
And your petitioners will ever pray.
Dated this 25th day of April, 1903.
I am perfectly satisfied that, if the attention of the imperial authorities were drawn to the peculiar disabilities under which our Cauadian soldiers were placed in view of the conditions of the regulations, some mitigation of them will be ordered, so that these men may obtain this much-coveted medal. I should like to know from the government if this petition was received, if it was forwarded to the impfrial authorities through the proper channels, and if any recommendation or any request was made by His Excellency to the imperial authorities that the regulations for the issuing of the King's medal might be altered to the extent suggested to His Excellency in connection with the service of the Canadian volunteers ? I repeat that I am sure it was not the intention of the imperial authorities to frame the regulations in such a way that our Canadian soldiers, who did such splendid service in the South African war, should be excluded from this honour. If the government have not taken action, I think they should do so, in order that this invidious distinction may not be perpetuated. I am sorry the Minister of Militia and Defence (Hon. Sir Frederick Borden) is not present. I gave him notice of my intention to bring this matter up on going into supply, and had hoped to receive from him information as to whether the petition had been received and what action had been taken, and, if it was forwarded, whether any answer has been received.

I regret the absence of the Minister of Militia and Defence. In his absence I would not feel at liberty to make any statement on the subject referred to by the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Clarke). But I will see to it that his attention is called to the matter, and, if any action has been taken, the information will be given to tbe hon. gentleman (Mr. Clarke) at a later stage.

I would like to say a word in support of what has been said by the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Clarke). There can he no question, that the regulation which provides for the issue of the King's medal to those who have served eighteen months in South Africa was meant to cover the case of those who enlisted a second time. I believe that all the colonial contingents were enlisted for a year's service. It is merely the fact that Canada is more distant than the other colonies that shuts our men out from this honour, whereas the very fact of that distance entitles them all the more to the honour, if it is to be given to any. I am sure that shutting our men out was the furthest from the thought of the imperial authorities and I have every confidence that if the matter is placed before them the oversight will be rectified to the advantage and to the credit of those amongst our people who deserve it. I take the opportunity of speaking on this subject because from the constituency which I represent more men went to South Africa than from any other constituency in the Dominion of Canada, and therefore, I believe there are more of my constituents interested in this matter, possibly, than those of any other member of the House. I know personally a number of men who were out in the first Canadian Mounted Rifles, and also in the third contingent who took part in the battle of Hart's

River, the final battle of the war, the one which practically decided the war-and it is no news, I presume, to members of this House that, in the estimation of those competent to judge, it was very largely the presence of the Canadians at that battle which produced the result which was achieved by that battle and in closing the war. Before sitting down, I would like to say that there was a Canadian corps which did serve throughout the war with very considerable distinction. I refer to the Canadian Scouts, organized at first by Captain, Howard, and afterwards commanded by Captain, or Major, Ross. I do not know whether the Canadian authorities have taken any cognizance of this corps or not; but it was known as the ' Canadian Scouts.' It was principally composed of Canadians, though not altogether, and it served with the greatest possible distinction for the longest possible term. And, certainly, while I do not think that anything we can do can add to their credit, I am strongly in favour of doing what we can to secure for ourselves as much credit as possible from their very gallant and distinguished actions.

I would like to add a word in support of what has been brought before the House by my hou. friend from West Toronto (Mr. Clarke) and supported by my hon. friend from Alberta (Mr. Oliver). It seems to me that a very good case might be made out-has been made out-for these Canadians who served twice in South Africa. The fact that the war ended when it did, prevented them from coming within the terms of this regulation, notwithstanding that they had gone to South Africa for the purpose of giving a second term of service which would have brought them well within those terms. Under the circumstances, I hope the government will be able to make such representations as will do to these men what I believe is no more than justice by placing them in the list of those who are entitled to receive the medal.
Will the minister be good enough to tell us if the South African Constabulary will participate in the receipt of these medals ?
I will call the Minister of Militia and Defence's attention to my hon. friend's (Mr. Sproule's) question.

Railways and canals-Intercolonial railway- to strengthen bridges, $165,100.
You were to give full details about that.

I understood the hon. gentleman wished to have a statement in detail as to the bridges to be strengthened. Of this sum $77,000 is a revote standing over from last year. I have here a list of the names of the bridges, which is of some length, but I will read it if the hon. gentleman desires. The number of spans in each case is also given.
What is the total amount expended up to date, and what is the probable amount required to finish this work of strengthening ?

The statement is made up to January last, at which date these papers were prepared. The amount expended up to that date was $451,680. I have given the hon. gentleman the names of most of the bridges for which the additional amount of $87,000 is required. There is also a list of bridges which are to be doubled up, as it is described in the department. As respects this $77,000 revote the items are given as follows : Balance due on bridges tendered for $31,000; floors ditto, $4,000; painting ditto, $1,400; false work, $4,500; doubling up, $3,500; inspection, &c., $1,811.10. These items make $77,711, which is the revote of last year's estimate and the other items which I have read represent the items which make up the additional expense to $87,000.
Does that complete the whole work of strengthening ?
The deputy informs me that he thinks this will finish the work of strengthening these bridges.
What expense has been put upon the bridges at Torryburn and Brockville ?
The list I have read only refers to the bridges which it is expected to deal with during the present season and the money has not been expended yet.
Is there any estimate as to the probable cost ?
Not in tiie case of each separate bridge. The estimate is general.
That is a total amount required for strengthening these bridges of over $600,000.
$451,000 up to the end of January.
There has been some expenditure since that to which is added the appropriation in these estimates. The hon. gentleman's figures, I think, are about correct.
Will the hon. minister say how many bridges the department have on hand now that there are doubling up ?
The list contains seventeen bridges which are to be doubled up out of this vote.

Do we understand that $3,500 is for the strengthening of bridges 1 The hon. gentleman gave an item of $3,500 to cover the doubling up of bridges. He surely does not intend to say that that is going to cover all the cost of strengthening these bridges.

$3,500 has reference to moneys expended in doubling up in the past. It will not pay for this list that I have read. The list that I have read in detail is for the bridges to be doubled up out of these estimates.
Then you are only estimating $3,500 to be expended that way ?
The amount set apart for doubling up is $33,988.
Are all these repairs to bridges chargeable to capital account ?
This is not for repairs to bridges. It is really for the betterment of the road by the strengthening of the bridges, and is therefore chargeable to capital account.
Is the strengthening of the bridges being done because these bridges have become weakened by the lapse of years ?

It is because of the heavier locomotives and rolling stock which are required to pass over these bridges. Having increased the weight of the locomotives and rolling stock the bridges which were good in the past are not strong enough now to bear the additional weight.
Are they new bridges ?
Doubling up of course, means the taking of two bridges and putting them together. These are not new bridges, but they are good bridges.
Do you charge the cost of doubling up two bridges to capital account ?
Where one bridge is transferred from one place to another it is not charged to capital.

We want some details of the number of bridges which you are doubling up in that way and we would like to have in connecuon with that the reasons for doing this. This method is not adopted by other lines of railway very extensively. I have never heard of it before.

In the case of old bridges doubled up the amount charged to capital account is the cost of making the change, not the cost of the bridge itself. The bridge itself, having been charged to capital account originally, remains in capital account, but the new bridges are charged to capital account.
Would it be fair to charge that to capital account ?
If you take a bridge from one portion of the road and put it in another portion of the road you still have it on the road and you have lost nothing.
I mean the expense of doing this work.
Yes, I think the expense of the work of changing the bridge from one part of the road to an: other is fairly chargeable to capital account.

I think we should have some details as to what becomes of the bridges which are replaced on the road. Do they go into scrap or are they used elsewhere ? We want to know where credit is given for them.

In one or two cases these bridges are being transferred to the Prince Edward Island road and of course they are charged up against that road and credited to the Intercolonial Railway. Where the bridges are being doubled up they are still utilized on the road. I have asked the deputy minister whether any cases have occurred in which they have gone into scrap and he thinks not.
If you move a bridge and build a new oue and charge the expense of that to capital account that cannot be right.	.

I suppose it would be a proper thing that the value of the bridge occupying the place of the old bridge which is removed should be deducted from the capital charge. I take it that when a bridge is found on the main line insufficient to carry the weight of the heavier locomotives now in use and you have to remove it and put a stronger bridge on the main line, removing the old bridge to the branch, the charge should be credited with something Mr. FOWLER.
for the value of the bridge which is dispensed with on the branch.
That would be quite correct if the bridge were sold off the road. If the bridge remains in the service of the road and is made use of elsewhere, you still have its value for the road.

Yes, but if you do not make this substitution and have to replace the bridge on what I call the branch line for illustration, you have to do that out of revenue, and if you simply take a bridge from the main line and put it on the branch that will simply be relieving the working expenses to that extent ; so that, if you strengthen a bridge on the main line and take the old bridge to another point you save the working expenses of that line of what would be necessary to renew the bridge on the branch. There is always a charge made for that purpose against revenue, and it saves capital so much money.

I am advised that the bridges are used either for the doubling up process, or, in one or two cases they have been moved to Prince Edward Island. If you take two bridges and put them together they still remain on the road. It is not a question of renewing; it is simply adding to the equipment of the strength of the road, and in the new bridge you have so much additional capital on the road.

Perhaps I did not make myself quite understood to the Minister of Finance. If you renew a bridge on the Prince Edward Island Railway you would have to do it at the expense of revenue, but instead of renewing it at expense of the revenue you bring an old bridge from the main line and put it there. You charge the whole expense of increasing the strength upon the main line to capital. Surely revenue has gained by this manipulation, and revenue should bear some portion of that charge. The result of this is that revenue has escaped the charge of renewing in the case of the Prince Edward Island Railawy. I am quite sure the deputy minister would thoroughly understand that if he were keeping his accounts for an ordinary railway company.
The error in my hon. friend's statement is that lie asserts that this work in Prince Edward Island is renewal.
Certainly.
That is a fatal error. It is not a renewal; the bridge is used on a new line and properly charged to capital account.

All the same, if a bridge that has gone out of service but is still of value is taken off the main line, the capital

account should receive credit for tlie value of the bridge. A manufacturer would easily make that charge as a matter of bookkeeping. If you are building a new line in Prince Edward Island and had. to buy a bridge you would have to charge that to capital account, but the Minister of Finance goes to the main line of the Intercolonial Railway and gets that bridge for nothing.

What the hon. gentleman says should be done is just what has been done in this case. The bridge is taken from the Intercolonial Railway to Prince Edward Island, and it is charged against the Prince Edward Island road and credited in the Intercolonial Railway accounts against capital account.
If that is so it is all right.

The bridge having been taken off the Intercolonial Railway goes into the stores account, and when it is taken out of the stores account it is charged to the Prince Edward Island Railway. Is it credited then to capital account on the Intercolonial Railway ?
I am informed that it is.
Can the minister point to any place in the public accounts where a credit of that kind is shown ? I have never seen it.
My hon. friend could not well see it in this case because the transaction has not taken place yet.

But these things are going on for the last three years and we have been complaining that we cannot get at the truth as to whether these accounts are credited or not.
T'he MINISTER OF FINANCE. 1 am glad to assure my hon. friend that what he thinks ought be done is being done in this case.
Hon. Mr. ROSS (Victoria, N.S.) The Minister of Railways and Canals explained last year this bridge was taken from the Mira-miclii river and transferred to Hillsborough.
It would seem that any old bridge is good enough for Prince Edward Island. Has the minister the information he promised us as to what is being done with the approaches on the Hillsborough bridge ?

Stretch the short one.

How much has been charged for this particular bridge to the Prince Edward Island Railway and how much credited to the Intercolonial Railway, and where does that appear in the accounts ?

Yes.

I will get the information later.
How old is that bridge?

The bridge was built in 1876, but it is not right to say that any old bridge is good enough for Prince Edward Island. My hon. friend (Mr. Barker) is pointing out that it is a very valuable bridge and that we should be careful to charge it. The bridge is not strong enough for its present purpose but it is a perfectly good bridge and is perfectly adapted for the traffic on the Prince Edward Island Railway which is a narrow gauge line and does not require such a strength of bridge as the Intercolonial Railway.
Could I get any idea of. what is the difference in cost between that bridge and a new bridge ?
That is the same question as was asked by the hon. member (Mr. Barker).

It seems to me that it is very poor policy to take a bridge twenty-seven years old, and practically useless, and transport it to Prince Edward Island at great cost, and put it on a substructure costing half a million dollars or more. This amount is being charged up to Prince Edward Island, and when we come and ask for a few railway facilities or means of transportation across the straits, there is always the cry that Prince Edward Island is asking too much.
Not from this side.

Yes, from that side. I think it poor policy to send us second-hand stuff, which probably in a few years will have to be changed ; and, according to the manner of bookkeeping of the last few years, this will be charged up to capital account, and it will be detrimental to the Prince Edward Island Railway.
My hon. friend does not help his case by stating that the bridge is worn out and no good. That does not happen to be the fact, but it was essential to my hon. friend's case to put it that way.
From what part of the Intercolonial Railway was this bridge taken?
From the Miramiclii river. It has not yet been taken, but is to be taken.

This was a light bridge when it was constructed, and I understand that the ordinary life of an iron bridge under good care is fifty years. The bridge, which is over half worn out, you are placing on a superstructure that is costing the country an immense amount of money, and in twenty or twenty-five years you will have to replace it by a new bridge. As the hon. member for East Prince says, it is poor economy. AVhen you are building a new railway in Prince Edward Island, and when you are constructing a bridge across the Hillsborough river at a great expense to the country, the least you can do is to put new material into it. But it appears to be the policy of this government, and especially of the Department of Railways and Canals, to send any old bridge across to Prince Edward Island, where it will have to be renewed in a few years. That is a policy of which I disapprove, and in the name of the people I represent, I must protest against it.

The hon. gentleman has fallen into the same error as his friend from the other district in suggesting that this is a worn-out bridge. All I can say is that it is not an old bridge, and that the ordinary life of an iron bridge is very much longer than the term the hon. gentleman has mentioned. At any rate, I Hon. Mr. FIELDING.
am informed on competent authority that this is a stronger and better bridge than any new bridge which would be built for the railway at that point.
I want to ask these hon. gentlemen, do they want us to throw away this bridge and build two new bridges ?
I would suggest that the government use this bridge in doubling up the bridges on the Intercolonial Railway, and give us a new bridge on the Prince Edward Island Railway.
No, put it on the Grand Trunk Pacific.

I cannot understand how these bridges appear as a credit capital account on the Intercolonial Railway. First of all, if they are taken from the Intercolonial Railway they go into the stores' account, and they are afterwards used on the Prince Edward Island Railway. By what process of bookkeeping is credit given to the Intercolonial Railway capital account for the amount expended on the Prince Edward Island Railway ?
I am informed that the stores' account will show it.

That does not appear in the capital account of the Intercolonial Railway. The expenditure for the purpose of strengthening and renewing the bridges on the Intercolonial Railway within the last few years has been over 81,000,000, besides an expenditure for repairs on the different bridges of nearly $700,000. The department has been running heavy locomotives on the Intercolonial Railway during the last two or three years ; and how is it that the government risked the lives of the employees on the railway during that time if these bridges were not sufficient to sustain the locomotives ? I suggested that if the bridges were not strong enough to bear the locomotives, new bridges should be built in the first place. But after the purchase of these heavy locomotives, and after they have been running three or four years, here is an expenditure of over $1,000,000 for the purpose of building new bridges and strengthening old ones. We have had no explanation as yet in regard to capital account.
The! MINISTER OF FINANCE. I thought that was made quite clear.
It is clear, I suppose, to the Finance Minister. The bridges, after they are removed, are put into the stores' account.
And credited there to capital account.
No, credited to the stores' account.

I am advised that this bridge, when it goes to Prince Edward Island, will be credited to the capital account of the Intercolonial Railway and charged to the capital account of the Prince Edward Island Railway.

I understand, from the statement of the hon. Finance Minister, that it is the intention that this particular bridge or material which is sent to Prince Edward Island shall be credited to the Intercolonial Railway. The Minister cannot tell us that that is done in any other particular case, and he cannot show that it will be done in this case-because the change is yet to be made. Now, the bridges are put into the stores' account when they are removed from the railway. I quite understand that the stores, having received this bridge along with $1,000,000 or $2,000,000 of other material, may issue bridges or anything else, and charge something to expense account and something to capital account. That must have been going on for years, and what I would like to understand is this. When we find year after year a sum put into the public accounts as charged to capital account, is that a charge of everything that is put in, or is it only a balance that is charged after crediting certain things and deducting the credits ?

In the case of an item on capital account, where there is to be a deduction later, we would have to take the full vote on capital account to enable us to have the money to buy the material ; but when the material enters into the actual construction of the road, then the account is credited with the proceeds of the article to be sold, and only the balance is charged to capital account.

What I understand is this: Supposing $5,500,000 has been expended on capital account in the actual operations of the year and $500,000 is credited the item for such things as these, what appears in the public accounts is only the difference between $5,500,000 and $500,000. In other words you only charge up $500,000.

That would be correct. But you might have to take a larger appropriation, in the first instance, to enable you to buy the goods. In the statement of the account later, it would be as the hon. gentleman has1 said.

Eet me suggest this. It would be of very great value to the House if the Department of Railways and Canals would show in its capital account the gross amount expended on capital and the credits on account of capital, so that we would see clearly that such items as these are credited to capital and only the net expenditure actually charged. I have over and over again in the last three years endeavoured to get at the facts, but I have never yet been able to ascertain that in any individual case
a credit has been given. The hon. gentleman can only tell us now that it is intended to be given in this case. He cannot tell of any particular case where such a credit has been actually given. It is most desirable that in future the railway reports should show the gross expenditure on capital account and what credits are deducted, difference being in the amount actually charged against capital account.

It looks to me as if the suggestion of my hon. friend has much to commend it. I would not like to commit myself too hastily, but I shall talk it over with the officials of the department. I do not see on the surface why the hon. gentleman's suggestion should not be carried out.
It would be of great advantage to the country.
But the hon. Finance Minister says it has been done already.
The lion.* geutleman's suggestion is that it should be shown in the account as well as done.

$500,000 is voted for the purpose of building a bridge. The whole amount is expended upon the bridge, but there is $50,000 from the old bridge, which ought to be credited to the new structure, but which goes into the stores account. By what process is credit given back again to the construction of that bridge or does it ever appear in any of the books ?

The hon. member for Hamilton tells me it does not, and I must not contradict him. I am sure it does appear in the stores account. The only question is whether it could not be shown in the manner he suggests. I am sure it does appear in the stores account.
No doubt it does but not in the capital account.
But for these credits the capital account would be so much larger.

I think the hon. minister will admit that no person can take the public accounts and say whether anything has been credited or not. There is a certain sum charged as expenditure on capital account, but there is nothing to show whether that expenditure was half as much more and was reduced to the amount charged.

As I understand the position, assuming that $100,000 was expended on a new bridge on the Intercolonial Railway and $10,000 received for the old bridge, instead of charging $100,000 to capital account, they only charge $90,000. If that is the method pursued, the result is correct, but it does not show the amount actually expended and the amount credited, and I agree with the hon. member for Hamilton that that ought to be shown.

I would like to know the total amount expended for the strengthening of bridges and putting In new bridges on account of these new locomotives. The total amounts expended on the Restigouche and the Miramichi bridges are two independent items. Add the two together and the amount expended on the other. I think it must be over $1,000,000.
The total amount is' made up to the 31st of January last. We have not the figures to the close of the fiscal year. Leaving out the bridges at Miramichi and at Restigouche, the amount is $461,680.
That is what the hon. gentleman said before. Then there is the vote of $165,000 to be added to that, and the hon. gentleman says that will complete the repairs on those bridges.
I stated rfhat this appropriation for the year will probably finish the work, but the general manager says it will take another year. There will be something further to be done.
You do not know what the amount is ?
I have not the estimates at haud.
For the total repairs of bridges ?
For strengthening the bridges ?

I have always understood that the department makes an estimate of the probable cost of strengthening bridges on the Intercolonial Railway. Will the hon. gentleman tell us what is the estimate cost of strengthening these bridges ?
There was an estimate made by the general manager and the recollection of my deputy is that it was about a million and a quarter dollars.
Surely there must be some mistake. That includes the bridges at Restigouche and Miramichi ?

The estimate is substantially correct-over a million dollars, including the large bridges as well as the process of doubling up. It would be subject to some deduction if bridges were sold off the road, but that has not yet been done, most of them being used In doubling up.

Then the department in making up these estimates would estimate what it would cost to strengthen the old bridges and what it would cost to buy the new bridges. Could the hon. gentleman tell us the items of these two classes of work ?
I do not give the hon. gentleman (Mr. Ingram) that information at the present time.

I have not yet understood the method of bookkeeping in dividing these items between capital and revenue accounts. Suppose a bridge costs $50,000 and $1,000 to put it in place, and it is to be replaced with a bridge costing $100,000, which it will cost $2,000 to put in place. Surely it cannot be said that the $1,000 spent in placing the original bridge is not lost ? At least $1,000 of the cost of putting in the new bridge should be charged to revenue.
I am afraid I have not understood my hon. friend's (Mr. Lefurgey's) question.
If it costs $1,000 to put the first bridge there, and you are taking that up, you have lost $1,000.
A good deal depends upon what you do with it.
But the expense of putting it there is lost. Either that, or, what would amount to the same thing, the same amount in the cost of putting in the new bridge should be charged to revenue.
Even if that were correct, it would not be a large item.
If you were putting in a hundred bridges, it would amount to $100,000. Of course, that is not large in these times.

The question raised by my hon. friend (Mr. Lefurgey) involves a point that we have been discussing for the last two or three years. Supposing a bridge as originally put in costs $1,000 and it is being removed and a bridge costing $5,000 is to be put in its place. The question is what is to be done with the original charge of $1,000. The revenue should be charged with whatever is necessary for the work up to its original value, and capital should stand the difference and also the $4,000 of the betterment. The objections that I have been trying to press upon the government are these. In the past the government have been practically adding the whole $1,000 to revenue account, and revenue has not been charged anything for superintendence. Suppose that this bridge costing $1,000 in the course of time becomes worth only $500, revenue should be charged with $500 and capital should be credited with $500 against the new one.

According to the statement of the minister it will require $1,250,000 to do this work. I should judge from the estimates for this year that he expects that the expenditure for the year will be $1,000,000, and it will require some $200,000 more to complete the work. How

was it then, that the minister made the statement last year or the year before that the total expenditure would be only about $000,000. [DOT]

The figures are certainly in excess of those the hon. gentleman mentions. I do not recall what the minister said. In view of the figures, $000,000 would fall very short. I think there must have been some misunderstanding as to what the minister said.
That would be far short of the actual
Just about half.

Before we pass this item, I would like the committee to fully understand the method of bookkeeping of the Intercolonial in this matter. I think the minister has acknowledged that the illustration I gave of the bridges is practically the way they are keeping their capital accounts. The Intercolonial charges to capita] many items such as a man in keeping his accounts of his own business would charge to the expenses. That being so it can easily be understood how the Minister of Railways and Canals has been able to show a surplus on the Intercolonial. If the people fully understand this, they will certainly condemn the administration for this attempt to deceive them by their method of bookkeeping.
Intercolonial Railway-air brakes to freight cars, $25,000.

The minister promised us, when this item was under discussion before, that he would give us a full account of how many freight cars were to be furnished with air brakes, and the cost. AVe would like to know also whether this is done under contract or whether there is a supply on hand.

The contractor is the Westinghouse Air Brake Company of Hamilton, Ontario. The total number of freight cars, June 30th, 1902, was 9,689. The number equipped with air brakes at that time was 5,568; so that there remained to be equipped 4,121. There were equipped in the year 1902-3, 449 cars, so that at tlie end of the year there remained to be equipped, 3,672 cars. The average cost per car is about $50.
AVhen will this work be completed, and what will it cost ?
About one-third of the total number remain to be equipped, so it will take several years.
What is the contract price ?
I am informed that is the schedule price which the Westinghouse establishment charges to all railways.
AATiat is the cost per car for the air brake, and what is the cost of the draw-bar ?
About $50 per car for the air brake, and $40 for the draw-bar.
The ex-Minister of Railways and Canals last year stated that the air brakes would cost about $40 and the draw-bars $25. There ought to be some reliable figures.
Perhaps the difference arises from the fact that the one item includes labour of putting on the brakes, while the other does not.

The minister says there are 9,609 freight cars. Is that the total
stock-list of freight cars ?
Yes.

Well, there are several hundred freight cars out of service that will have to be purchased or rebuilt. Does the hon. gentleman include these in the number for which he is going to take a special vote? -because nowadays, the hon. gentleman knows, he can buy them equipped with all these appliances. I would like him to explain that, so that we may not be putting four or live hundred too many on one side of the account.
The fig-gures I quoted include every car on the list.

Then the cars out of service, there are 400 or 500 of them, will be bought as new cars, and they will be bought, no doubt, with the full equipment of modern cars. The hon. gentleman will not want to buy the Westinghouse equipment to put upon them as if they were old cars.

I am told that when the cars get out of service they will be rebuilt in the shops and charged to renewals, with the exception of the airbrakes, which will be charged to capital in as much as the old cars did not have the-air-brakes.
This is an opportune time, as the general manager is here, to ask why they have not already been dealt with in that way instead of the government buying new cars.

It is because of the increasing business of the

road they need both, not only to buy new ones but to repair old ones.

Perhaps the minister could tell us why these cars that are out of service, and have been out of service year after year, have not been restored instead of buying new cars. The hon. gentleman knows there would have been a very large addition to the working expenses of the railway. But by not doing that and by buying new ears, there has been no addition to the working expenses of the railway, and there has been a large addition to the debt of the country.

The manager informs me that they were doing all they could in this direction, they are constantly buying new cars as well as constantly repairing and improving old ones, to the extent of their facilities.

The extent of their facilities seems to be getting behind, and we are paying year after year large sums to increase the equipment at Moncton to enable the department to do this work. I would like to point out that a far more profitable answer is this, that if the department had replaced these cars in their shops, the charge would have been to working expenses ; but by buying them from the United States and elsewhere, it has gone to capital account; and the company is supposed to have been making a profit on the road when there has really been a large loss.

I am advised that the proportion of these cars which are out of service now is not larger than that of other railroads. They have perhaps in the past not been able to overtake them, but they have now caught up, and there is not more than the usual proportion of cars out of service.

Two years ago I went into that question particularly, and I cited the reports of the Grand Trunk Railway and other companies as to their equipment of locomotives, and showed that the Grand Trunk Railway, two years ago, I think, it was, was actually ahead of its stock list, while the Intercolonial Railway was 700 cars behind.
That was correct a few years ago, but I am glad to be able to say we have done better since.
No, you have done worse.
What is the capacity of the box cars they have been buying ?
60,000 and SO,000 pounds, the size of modern cars.
What has been done under the recommendation of Mr. Muhlfeld as to the equipment of certain cars and locomotives with what was known as the Chapman ball bearing apparatus ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext: Nothing has been done.

Was anything done on the report submitted by Mr. Muhlfeld ?
The'MINISTER OF FINANCE. He made a report, but the officials tell me it was not acted upon.
Then there are none of these ball bearings in use now on any of the locomotives or rolling stock of the Intercolonial ?
None.
While dealing with that phase of the question, I would like to know what has been done with Mr. Cleveland's patent for cylinders ?
It is being used on several locomotives at the present time.

I understand Mr. Cleveland has had his patent put on some 18 locomotives on the Intercolonial, they have been on for some time, and that gentleman can get no information as to whether they were regarded as satisfactory.
I understand that the reason why they have not furnished information as to the success of these appliances is that the officials wish to test them for a longer time.
They have been on for some years, I understand.

The first was put on three years ago. These gentlemen have been making changes in the appliance since that time and improvements as they claim and the officials have not felt justified in giving any report up to the present time.

And no report as to how it acted in the first place or as to these improvements from time to time ? I understand that in the state of Michigan there is a gentleman who has got out a patent which is becoming a very serviceable one. By reason of using it the locomotive consumes less fuel and greater speed is attained and the patent is becoming very valuable. It does seem to me strange that after these gentlemen have submitted this appliance to test on the Intercolonial for three years they could get no report upon it. It is not fair to these men and there must be some cause for not giving a report.

I am informed that the people interested in this appliance have received some reports as to what is being done, but they would like a more general report. They have reports from time to time as to the fuel consumption, &c., which are important elements in the matter, but they have been applying to the department for a general report, no doubt,

with the desire, should it prove satisfactory, that they should supply some more of these appliances.

When may we expect that they will be able to get that report ?
The* MINISTER OF FINANCE. One of the gentlemen concerned in the pateut, I am informed, has spent most of his time at Moncton up to a comparatively recent date and is perfectly familiar with the operation of the appliance. He was there observing it himself and therefore did not need any report.

I am bound to say that if I read the letter that I have in my possession, it would ensure the hon. Minister of Finance that this gentleman has become very tired waiting around Moncton to get a report. I think if I read the letter it would raise the hair of the hon. gentleman' head, but I do not feel like doing so because I do not think it would be a good thing to put on record. He complains very bitterly that he cannot obtain any report from the Intercolonial in reference to this test, that he can get no satisfaction at all and that the officials of the Intercolonial Railway simply Ignore him. There are three gentlemen interested in this patent, one of them is in San Francisco and another is in Toronto. One of these gentlemen was here endeavouring to get some information, but he could get no satisfaction from the department and he was forced to leave Ottawa. He is a poor man without the means to enable him to remain around and I think he has hardly been treated fairly. If his patent is no good he should be told so at once.
Does the hon. gentleman mean that the gentleman who was recently here was the one who has been at Moncton ?
Yes.
I understand that there are several parties connected with this patent and I am not sure that they all take the same view.
Who are the other gentlemen connected with it ? There are three of them, are there not ?
There are Teterson and Cleveland and there are several members of the concern. There are two Tetersons and two Clevelands.

I am informed that the patent office only recognized two-Mr. Cleveland and Mr. Peterson. The trouble, Mr. Cleveland tells me, is that there are some parties associated with the concern in Moncton, some gentlemen who have become interested in it in a way, Mr. Cleveland thinks, that is causing it to be a case of freeze-out, and Mr. Cleveland objects to being frozen out. Yet, he and the other two control the patent as far as the patent office is concerned.
'The MINISTER OF FINANCE. They will have to settle the patent question among themselves.
I think the Intercolonial Railway should give them some satisfaction.
Is it the intention of the department to go on and instal this Chapman double ball bearing apparatus on certain locomotives and cars on the report of Mr. Muhlfeld 1

The
privilege has been accorded to these parties to make a trial of this apparatus, but they have not so far availed, themselves of it.
At their own expense ?
Yes, there is no present understanding as to any further action.
Have you much of a supply of these air-brakes on hand ?
There are some on hand.
Not a large quantity ?

I think not.
Sir. INGRAS1. Can the hon. minister say definitely whether the estimate he is making for the air-brake and draw-bar includes the labour or not ?

This $50 I have quoted as the cost of the air-brakes does include the labour of putting them in.
Sir. INGRAS1. And the $40 for drawbars also includes the labour ?
The S1INISTER OF FINANCE. Yes.

I find by a circular issued by this company that the arrangement is not as the hon. minister has stated it to the committee. The hon. member for SVest York (Sir. Campbell) is president of this company and with the view of selling stock they have issued a prospectus purporting to give a copy of a report by Sir. Sluhlfeld. It says :
The railway to pay the cost for the expense for the application of the equipment only to such an amount as may be occasioned by the removal of the present equipment. If, after one year's continuous service, the equipment has demonstrated that it can fulfil all of the requirements, in accordance with the claims made for it by the inventor, and the company who may control the invention, the railway to pay the additional amount to defray the cost for the initial application.
The S1INISTER OF FINANCE. Is my hon. friend reading from a prospectus ?
From the prospectus which is purporting to give a copy of the report of Mr. Muhlfeld, superintendent of machinery and rolling stock.
Mr. Mulh-feld has not been in the service of the Intercolonial for some time.

He was in the service at the time this report was written, in May, 1902. Is that still the standing of this company or is the company sailing under false colours in making this publication to the people ?

I am afraid I cannot add anything to what I have already stated. The officials of the department state that the privilege was accorded to this company of making a trial at their own expense, but that they have not availed themselves of it.
Then this report is misleading ?
I do not say anything about that. I do not form any opinion as to the report.
Do I understand that the privilege is cancelled or is it still open on the terms of the report of Mr. Muhlfeld ?

That will have to be considered if they should make an application. It is intended that they should have the privilege of having a full test made of this apparatus, and if they make an application to us we will consider it.
Is the report correct in stating that the department were to pay as set forth in the report which I have read?
The understanding of the department was that the trial was to be made at the expense of the company.
Then the report is misleading.
I do not say anything about the report.
Is not the cost of putting on air-brakes cheaper now than it was a year or two ago Two years ago the minister said that these air-brakes cost $70 each and now we are told they only cost $50.
I cannot explain that. Things have not become very much cheaper, the good times continue.

Is it the reduction of duty on the air ?
Some lion. MEMBERS. Hear, hear.
Labour is higher now than it was two years ago ; perhaps the reason is that yon are buying a larger quantity and are getting them cheaper.
The prices may vary a little, but I have no information that would enable me to explain the difference between $50 and $70.
Which is correct, the $50 or the $70?
I can only be responsible for the $50.
When did you first commence buying air-brakes from the Westing-house Company at Hamilton ?

The Railway Department has had relations with the Westingliouse Company for a long time, and since they have established themselves at Hamilton we have been doing business with them. That may be two or three year ago or perhaps longer.
I suppose it is another evidence that the protective tariff brings manufacturers to Canada.
There is no doubt that the manufacturing industries of Canada have prospered enormously under the administration of the present government. I cannot deny it.
But that is due to the tariff of the old government.
But lion, gentlemen opposite are complaining that this is a wretched tariff we have now ; I cannot understand them at all.
Perhaps they are cheaper because they are manufactured in Canada.
I cannot say. It is since this government came into power that most of these things happen in that way.
Is not the explanation that that since the Westinghouse Company came into Canada they have entered into a new contract with the government at a reduced price ?	-

I have no information as to that.
To exchange draw-bars on freight cars, $46,-
000.

The cost per car is $40. The total number of freight cars on June 30, 1902 was 9,689 ; the number equipped with master car builders couplers was 5,743 to June 30, 1902 : there remained to be changed 3,946 ; there were changed last year, 1,008 and there remained to be changed 2,938. This vote is supposed to deal with 1,150 cars.

As I have the report of the Railway Department here now, I find that the exact number of cars out of service to the end of June, 1902, is 571 ; I said 560 from memory. The minister thought they were improving, but the report shows that at the end of the previous year the number out of service was 361, so that lie has gone 210 to the bad during the year.
I am assured that in the report for the present year the situation will be improved.
Distance lends enchantment to the view.
Are you taking them off one class of cars and putting them on another ?
We are exchanging the old fashioned coupler for the modern appliance.
Are you charging the whole cost to capital?
Yes ; the old ones are used in repairs to the old cars.
That will not do.
It is a fact.
That is too thin.
On what principle do you charge changing draw-bars to capital ?
It is a decided betterment.
But a thing of that kind is never charged to capital.
Betterment is one thing and charging the whole cost is a very different thing.
Do you manufacture them in the shops at Moncton ?
Some have been bought in Walkerville, some in Montreal, and some in the United States.
What becomes of the old draw-bars ?
They are used in repairing old cars.
But if they are smashed they cannot be used.
Then they go into the scrap heap.

And if they do go into the scrap heap does not the minister see that revenue is bound to replace them ? He has no right to charge their replacement to capital. He has 900 old draw-bars, he throws them into the scrap heap, and he has not charged anything to revenue. The revenue of the company has got to replace the old ones, and if they are not worth replacing you must charge the difference between what it would cost to replace the old ones, and the cost of the new ones to capital account. Your revenue has to bear the expense necessary to replace the old ones.

I would like to know what railway system in Canada or the United States follows a system similar to that followed on the Intercolonial Railway?
Or is this system followed on the Intercolonial Railway because the management can get a vote of government money whenever they want it ? It is easier to buy new material than to replace the old, and charge it to capital account under these circumstances.
I cannot answer that.
Well, I think if a little common sense were applied that system would not be adopted merely because the money is voted so easily.
[DOT] We do not find that the money is easily voted. We get it with great difficulty.
The managers of other railways do not get their money so easily.

The hou. minister is not entitled to say that he cannot answer for that, because for two or three years past he has voted squarely in the House for the very things we are contending for, and he must take the responsibility for it.
I take the responsibility of it ; but what I cannot answer is as to the affairs of other companies.

Surely the superintendent can give the information. Where are all these Master Car Builders' Associations we have heard so much about? Surely the government railways are not run without the managers having an interchange of ideas with the managers of other companies. Surely they are not conducting this railway on their own ideas, and not inquiring how other railways are conducted. Will the hon. minister say that any officer of the Intercolonial Railway associates with the officers of other railways and attends the meetings which are held occasionally with a view to finding out the best way to conduct the railway? I am afraid there is something wrong about this whole business.
Intercolonial Railway-new machinery for locomotive and car shops, $8,000.

The details of this are as follows : Ferguson flue welding furnace, operated by oil ns fuel, $200; 300 horse-power engine, $3,000 ; buzz planer, $120; 100 horse-power engine, $1,500; turning lathe to take 16 feet between centres, $1,600; little giant pneumatic drill, $40; combination cold saw cutting-off machine, $1,000; belting, &c., $540. The machinery asked for is of the latest and most improved design, and is to facilitate the repairs of locomotives and cars. The present engines are too small to furnish power required to run shops with the new machinery placed and enlargements made, and it is proposed to replace them witli engines asked above. The present engines will be used at other points on the line.
Was the .$10,000 voted last year all expended for machinery?

Yes.
lion. Mr. HAGGART. What is the total cost of the machinery in these shops now?

I cannot give that to the hon. gentleman, but I will give it to him at a later stage.
Intercolonial Railway-to equip ten passenger cars with Pintsch gas apparatus, $8,000.
This is found to be the latest and most satisfactory system. The cost is $800 per car, and we propose to equip 10 cars.
How many remain to be equipped ?
The total number to be equipped to the end of the year will be 20. That will complete the work.
When you discard one system of lighting on the Intercolonial Railway and introduce another, you charge the cost to capital account?

The apparatus for the Pintsch system is entirely new, and is charged to capital account. All the new cars are fitted with that apparatus; and when we take an old car which is only fitted with a gas lamp and put in the Pintsch system, that is charged to capital' account.
Many of the cars were lighted with electric light.
There were a number of cars equipped with electric light on the storage battery system; but that was found to be inconvenient and not economical, and we are adopting the Pintsch system instead.
You put out the electric light and put in this, and charge the whole to capital account?
Yes.

Then, the principle on the Intercolonial Railway seems to be this, that if the management in one season fancy a particular lamp and buy it, and the next year think another kind is more suitable, they turn out the first and put in the new one, and charge both to capital account. Is that the principle? If it is, it is a most extraordinary one.
Is this a cheaper system of lighting than electricity?
Yes, the officials think it is decidedly cheaper than the system of a storage battery. Some railways are introducing dynamos, but they have not been introduced on the Intercolonial Railway.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext: Does it cost less to fit up a car with the Pintsch system than with the electric light apparatus?
Yes. that is the opinion of the officials.
How many of these cars are fitted with electric light?
I cannot give the hon. gentleman the number, but I will get that at a later stage.
What is the nature of this new system ? Does it generate gas ?

It is a system of cylinders and piping-a storage system of gas. The gas is made at the shops in Moncton and stored in these cylinders and pipes. It is called the Pintsch gas system, which is used on most of the railways that do not use the electric lights. It is made from oil.
It is very costly, $800 per car. Is it expensive to keep up afterwards ?
The chief expense is in the fitting up.

I do not think there is much dispute about the Pinsch system being a good one. But I think the real question is this. If the officials of a railway, who may change from year to year their ideas with regard to the kinds of lamps to be used in the cars, are allowed to have their way, we will have all sorts of experiments tried, according to the fancies of the gentleman, who for the time being is the superintendent. If you adopt the ordinary principle that when officials want to try from one year to the other, which is the better system, they must do it at the expense of their current account, they will have some motive to be economical and careful, but it is almost historical that when you allow officials to expend anything they like and charge it to capital, they will say : Why should we not expend the money so long as parliament votes it. There is no check whatever and no inducement to officials to be economisal and careful so long as they can get whatever they please without adding one cent to their working expenses. The only safety in the operation of a road, whether run by a government or a company, is to have the officials who are responsible run up their working expenses by every purchase they make and not have these purchases treated as an additional mortgage on the property.
Rolling stock, $637,000.
I prop ise to reduce that to $327,000.
We should have an explanation why the amount was put in the first instance at $037,000 and why it was subsequently reduced ?
If I give an explanation of the sum I ask the House
to rote, tlie lion, gentleman should be content.
Certainly not.
